marrow__ANAT_CH37_Q001.takeaway: The nipple is supplied chiefly by T4; the mammary gland is a modified sweat gland on pectoral fascia with multiple arterial sources.
marrow__ANAT_CH37_Q001.displayText: The nipple is supplied by the anterior branch of the lateral cutaneous branch of T4 (4th intercostal nerve), so the statement that it is supplied by the 6th intercostal nerve is incorrect. The breast is innervated by anterior and lateral branches of the 4th to 6th intercostal nerves (sensory and sympathetic efferent). The mammary gland is a modified sweat gland lying on the deep pectoral fascia over pectoralis major. It receives blood from the internal thoracic artery, lateral thoracic artery and lateral branches of posterior intercostal arteries.

rationales.b: This is true: the gland overlies pectoralis major on deep pectoral fascia.
rationales.c: This is true: internal thoracic branches contribute to breast blood supply.

marrow__ANAT_CH37_Q002.takeaway: The axillary tail is the gland axillary process and passes through the deep-fascial foramen of Langer.
marrow__ANAT_CH37_Q002.displayText: The axillary tail of Spence is the axillary process of the mammary gland. It passes through the foramen of Langer. The foramen of Langer is an opening in the deep fascia through which the superolateral quadrant is prolonged toward the axilla. It lies along the inferolateral edge of pectoralis major and may extend through the deep fascia up to the apex of the axilla.

rationales.a: Foramen of Winslow is the epiploic opening between peritoneal spaces, not an opening in breast fascia.
rationales.b: The quadrangular space is an intermuscular passage transmitting axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral vessels.
rationales.d: The triangular space transmits circumflex scapular vessels; it is unrelated to the breast axillary process.

marrow__ANAT_CH37_Q003.takeaway: Breast tissue receives branches from internal thoracic, lateral thoracic, thoracoacromial/superior thoracic and posterior intercostal arteries; the axillary trunk itself is not a direct source.
marrow__ANAT_CH37_Q003.displayText: The direct blood supply of the breast does not include the axillary artery itself. Major sources shown in the source table are lateral thoracic artery to the lateral breast; medial mammary branches of the internal thoracic artery to the medial breast; pectoral branches of thoracoacromial and superior thoracic arteries to the superior breast; and 2nd-4th posterior intercostal arteries to the base. The veins generally correspond with the arteries and drain into axillary and internal thoracic veins. The source notes that the left internal mammary (internal thoracic) artery is preferred for coronary artery bypass grafting because it has superior short- and long-term patency compared with saphenous-vein grafts.

marrow__ANAT_CH37_Q004.takeaway: Resting alveolar epithelium is cuboidal and becomes columnar during lactation; the other listed breast-tissue statements match the source.
marrow__ANAT_CH37_Q004.displayText: Alveolar epithelium is cuboidal in the resting phase and columnar during lactation, so the statement that it is columnar in the resting phase is false. Fibrous stroma forms septa (suspensory ligaments of Cooper) anchoring skin and gland to pectoral fascia; it forms the major part of the gland but is absent beneath the areola and nipple. During development, thoracic ectodermal ingrowths form 15-20 solid buds that canalize into lactiferous ducts and secretory alveoli. Contraction of myoepitheliocytes facilitates passage of milk along the ducts. The 15-20 lactiferous ducts converge toward the nipple and form lactiferous sinuses.

rationales.d: Myoepithelial contraction helps propel milk along the ducts.

marrow__ANAT_CH37_Q005.takeaway: Mammary cells release protein by merocrine secretion and milk lipid by apocrine secretion.
marrow__ANAT_CH37_Q005.displayText: Mammary gland cells secrete milk protein (casein) by merocrine secretion, while milk lipid is secreted by apocrine secretion. Therefore breast-milk secretion combines apocrine and merocrine mechanisms. The source summarizes gland secretion types: merocrine - vesicles fuse with plasma membrane and release their contents; apocrine - the apical portion of the cell is pinched off for secretion (examples include milk fat, atypical sweat glands and ceruminous glands); holocrine - the entire gland cell disintegrates to liberate secretion (e.g., sebaceous glands). Eccrine sweat glands were formerly classified as eccrine but are now placed under merocrine.

marrow__ANAT_CH37_Q006.takeaway: Lymph from the superolateral breast commonly reaches anterior (pectoral) axillary nodes first, making them sentinel nodes for this drainage route.
marrow__ANAT_CH37_Q006.displayText: Lymphatics from the upper outer quadrant of the breast drain first into the anterior axillary lymph nodes, which therefore function as sentinel nodes in this setting. A sentinel node is the first lymph node receiving lymphatic drainage from a tumor and may be removed during surgery for histopathological assessment of metastasis. Axillary nodes receive more than 75% of breast lymph. The source also classifies axillary nodes relative to pectoralis minor: Level 1 (low nodes) below pectoralis minor; Level 2 (middle nodes) behind the muscle; Level 3 (apical/upper nodes) between the upper border of pectoralis minor and lower border of clavicle. Nodes between pectoralis major and minor are interpectoral (Rotter's) nodes.

rationales.c: Supraclavicular nodes are not the first basin for the usual upper-outer-quadrant pathway.
rationales.d: Internal mammary nodes receive medial breast drainage rather than the common upper-outer route.

marrow__ANAT_CH37_Q007.takeaway: Peau d’orange follows subdermal lymphatic obstruction: edema expands skin tethered by Cooper ligaments and accentuates follicular/sweat-pore dimpling.
marrow__ANAT_CH37_Q007.displayText: The image shows the peau d'orange appearance of the breast. It occurs due to blockade of sub-dermal lymphatics and is one of the most conspicuous signs of breast cancer. Obstruction of lymphatic drainage produces edema of the breast, but the swollen skin remains tethered to the ligaments of Cooper; the sweat-gland and hair-follicle openings are pulled inward, producing the typical orange-peel appearance.

rationales.a: The described orange-peel texture is caused by lymphatic obstruction and edema, rather than simply direct skin metastasis.
rationales.b: Adherence/tethering of skin is supplied by Cooper ligaments; the source identifies lymphatic blockade as the initiating cause.
rationales.d: Cooper ligament infiltration can tether or retract skin, but does not account for the characteristic edema and pore retraction described here.
